summary:
Artvin stands under the national framework of Turkey, where hostility toward trans people has been organised into documented state policy rather than left as residual prejudice. Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record, and systematic attacks on the privacy of LGBT people.

The Erdoğan government has repeatedly justified its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. A draft legislative package that would effectively criminalise LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025; it had not been passed when reported, but its pending status has not stopped authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul shows that gap in practice. During 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

The passport-carrying rule compounds this. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated demands for an independent investigation came from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that Turkey places trans prisoners by registered sex, a trans man having been held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees rest on segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than a statement of current law.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft omnibus justice package, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with penalties of up to four years in prison, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with a requirement of permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. The package contains no province-specific provisions.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy, documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit state policy, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a "Year of the Family" banner creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and with regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at the report launch.

The surviving evidence for Artvin is entirely national-level and carries no provincial breakdown, so neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established here; the documented national picture applies in the province unchanged.
tangentialFactors:
The draft 11th Judicial Package illustrates a wider Turkish pattern in which enforcement runs ahead of legislation: the package was still unpassed in October 2025, yet GBT stops, documentation of trans women and public-institution instructions were already being applied under the "Year of the Family" banner. A visitor should expect conduct to be governed by administrative and police practice as much as by enacted statute.

Opposition to the draft comes from inside Turkish professional and civil society structures, not only from external monitors. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association are on record against it, and the Health Ministry's September 2025 recording change was contested online as an "LGBT opening", indicating active domestic dispute over the direction of policy.

The depth of the pattern predates the current government's measures. Human Rights Watch's 2008 findings on beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people, and the Truth Justice Memory Center's finding that violations have continued since 2015, place the 2025 escalation within a longer continuum rather than an isolated episode.

Comparable risk drivers elsewhere in Turkey, such as the Istanbul GBT stops and the Sincan Women's Prison death, are documented only in major urban and institutional settings; no equivalent reporting exists for Artvin in either a hostile or a protective direction.

Residents seeking transition-related care face the Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports: hospitals may no longer record the "other" option and e-reports are required, which profiles trans patients in official records.

Turkish citizens and residents held in custody are placed by registered sex, as confirmed in parliament on 12 December 2025, and LGBT detainees face strip searches, de facto solitary confinement, disrupted visits and ineffective complaints mechanisms according to the Prison Insider profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association.

The status of the 11th Judicial Package after the 29 October 2025 reporting is unresolved in this inventory; the sources establish that it was a leaked draft and had not been passed at that date, and nothing further is sourced.

Enforcement statistics in the inventory, including the 313 violations, 299 detention decisions and the roughly 20 women stopped in Istanbul, are national or Istanbul figures with no provincial allocation, so their distribution across Artvin is not sourced.
